threads.thread_goal: Align on current workflow, main issues, and project scope before design work.

messages.text:
Kicking off the rollout of our new outpatient check-in and triage process for project_title: Rollout of New Outpatient Check-in and Triage Process.
To get started, can everyone describe how check-in and triage currently work in their area and the main pain points they see? I will consolidate this into the current workflow map for T1 and then into A1.
It would help if you include: 1) what happens from patient arrival to nurse triage, 2) where delays usually appear, 3) any data or consent issues you notice.

From the nursing side, once the patient is called from the waiting room, we do a quick ID check, confirm reason for visit, and take vitals before deciding if they can wait or need faster attention.
Pain points I see:
- We often get incomplete intake forms, so we have to ask again about medications or allergies.
- There is no clear rule on when to escalate to the head nurse versus calling the physician directly.
- During busy hours, patients arrive faster than we can triage, so the waiting room gets crowded and people get anxious.

At the front desk, the current flow is roughly:
- Patient arrives and gives ID card.
- We look them up in the EHR, confirm contact details, and hand over a paper intake form.
- They fill it in the waiting area and bring it back to us.
- We check for missing fields quickly and then put the form in a tray for nursing.
Issues:
- People often skip insurance details or medication lists.
- If they do not speak the main language well, we lose time explaining the form.
- Sometimes we enter data into the EHR only after the nurse has already seen the patient, so information is not aligned.

Adding to what 196511 said, another detail at the desk:
- We do not have a clear rule on who enters which fields in the EHR. Sometimes the person who checked the patient in does it, sometimes the colleague who is free later.
- When it is busy, we just scan the paper form and postpone typing the data, which leads to errors later.
- We also do not have a standard way to record consent; some colleagues just tick a box in the system, others keep a signed paper in a folder.

From a quality perspective, the main issues I have seen in spot checks are:
- Inconsistent recording of consent and privacy notices.
- Missing mandatory identifiers in the EHR compared to the paper form.
- No routine check of how long patients wait between arrival and triage.
For A1 and T1, I suggest we mark clearly where checks should happen so we can later design a QC checklist that fits naturally into the flow.

Looking at this from a training and documentation angle, I notice that:
- New staff learn the process informally from whoever is on shift, so there are variations.
- We do not have a single visual overview of the steps from arrival to triage.
- There is no short guide for what to tell patients about waiting times and what information they will be asked.
Once A1 is drafted from T1, I can start thinking about how to turn it into simple training materials later.

Thanks all, this is very helpful. I will start mapping the current steps for T1 into A1 with:
- Patient arrival and ID check at front desk.
- Paper intake form completion and quick review.
- Data entry into EHR (sometimes delayed).
- Handover of forms to nursing.
- Nurse ID check, reason for visit, vitals, and triage decision.
Can you confirm if there are any shift-specific variations, for example evenings or weekends, that we should capture now?

On late shifts, we usually have only one person at the desk, so:
- The same person handles phone calls, arrivals, and printing forms.
- Data entry into the EHR is almost always delayed until there is a quiet moment.
- If there is a queue, we sometimes skip checking if the form is fully completed to avoid complaints about waiting.
I think this should be reflected in T1 so we do not design a process that only works when we have full staffing.

For nursing, on weekends we often have fewer nurses, so:
- One nurse may be doing both triage and some treatments.
- We sometimes ask patients to wait longer before vitals if there is an urgent case.
- There is no clear rule on how to prioritize follow-up visits versus new patients.
This might be important when we define what should stay unchanged in the first rollout, especially around emergency escalation.

Agree that emergency escalation should probably remain as is for the first rollout. We can still standardize documentation and timing around it, but changing clinical escalation paths might require more approvals.
For the project objectives, I suggest we focus on:
- Reducing average waiting time from arrival to triage.
- Increasing completeness of mandatory data fields and consent.
- Reducing discrepancies between paper forms and EHR entries.
We can later track these in A6 once we get to the pilot.

Those objectives make sense to me and they are measurable. For training design later, it would help if we also agree on a simple success message, for example:
- Patients understand what will happen next and how long it might take.
- Staff can describe the new steps consistently.
We can translate the more technical metrics into something easy to communicate during sessions.

Let me summarize what I am hearing so we can close on the main objectives for D1 and what stays unchanged for D2.
Proposed objectives:
1) Shorter and more predictable time from arrival to triage.
2) More complete and consistent intake data and consent, both on paper and in the EHR.
3) Fewer discrepancies between paper forms and EHR entries.
4) Clearer communication to patients about steps and waiting times.
For the first rollout, we keep the existing emergency escalation paths and clinical decision rules, and focus on standardizing check-in, documentation, and non-urgent triage steps.
Can everyone live with this as our starting point?

From the nursing side, I agree with keeping the current emergency escalation rules unchanged for now.
The objectives you listed also match what we need on the floor: less re-asking of questions and clearer expectations for patients.

Works for me as well. If we can reduce back-and-forth on incomplete forms and avoid double typing into the EHR, that will already be a big win at the desk.
I support the objectives and the idea of not touching emergency rules in this first phase.

Agree on the objectives and on keeping emergency escalation as is.
From the desk perspective, I would just add that we should also aim for clearer responsibility on who enters which data into the EHR, but that probably fits under the consistency objective.

I am aligned with the objectives and the scope limits.
For quality tracking later, I will translate these into a small set of indicators we can monitor during the pilot and early rollout, using A6.

Great, thanks everyone. I will finalize the current workflow map in A1 based on T1 with these objectives and constraints in mind.
Next I will share a first draft of the current vs future workflow so we can start designing improvements in the next thread.

threads.thread_goal: Design and validate the new workflow, forms, and triage protocol.

messages.text:
As a follow-up, I have drafted an updated workflow map in A1 based on T1, and 196511 and I prepared a first version of the standardized intake and consent forms for T2.
Also, 313168 has started outlining the triage protocol for T3.
Sharing here so we can review structure, mandatory fields, and triage steps together before we lock anything in.

On the intake and consent forms for T2 and A2, the structure is:
- Page 1: patient identifiers, contact details, insurance, preferred language.
- Page 2: reason for visit, current medications, allergies, key medical history.
- Separate consent section: data protection notice, consent for treatment, and consent for sharing data with other providers when needed.
Mandatory fields are marked with a star. I tried to keep the number of free-text fields low to reduce typing later into the EHR for T6.
Can you check if any critical clinical or legal items are missing before we move to formatting?

For the triage protocol draft in A3 and T3, I have outlined:
- Three urgency categories: immediate, urgent, routine.
- Criteria based on vitals, main complaint, and risk factors.
- Escalation paths: immediate cases go directly to the physician or emergency room; urgent cases are prioritized in the outpatient queue; routine cases follow normal scheduling.
I am less sure about the exact thresholds for some vitals and which symptoms should always trigger escalation. I would appreciate input, and we may need to validate with the head nurse before final approval.

From a quality and compliance angle, the intake and consent forms in A2 for T2 look generally solid.
A few suggestions:
- Make sure the consent section clearly separates mandatory legal notices from optional consents (for example, research use if applicable).
- Add a checkbox to confirm that the patient received the privacy notice.
- Align the list of mandatory identifiers with what the EHR requires in T6 so we do not create extra work.
If we agree on these adjustments, I am comfortable moving toward approval of the structure for D3, pending a quick review by the compliance officer.

From the front-desk side, the new A2 layout is clearer than the current form.
Two practical points:
- Could we group the fields we must type into the EHR first, so we can quickly check them at the desk?
- For the two languages, it would help to keep the layout identical so we do not get lost when switching.
Otherwise, I think the number of fields is manageable if we explain to patients why we need them.

Looking at A1 and A2 together, the flow seems coherent: arrival, identifiers, reason for visit, then triage.
For training later (T5), it would be useful if the form visually mirrors the steps in the workflow map, so staff can remember the order more easily.
On the consent text, I suggest we keep the language as simple as possible and avoid long paragraphs, especially since we will have it in two languages.

I can adjust A2 for T2 to:
- Separate mandatory legal notices from optional consents.
- Add a checkbox confirming that the patient received the privacy notice.
- Reorder fields so that the ones required in the EHR for T6 are grouped at the top.
Once I do that, we should be close to agreeing on the structure and mandatory fields for D3, subject to the compliance officer confirming the wording.

I will support with the EHR alignment for T6 by listing exactly which fields are mandatory in the system and checking that A2 matches them.
If we keep the structure stable after that, it will be easier to train front-desk staff and avoid local variations.

On the triage thresholds in A3 for T3, I propose we start with:
- Immediate: very abnormal vitals (for example, very low blood pressure, very high heart rate), chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or major bleeding.
- Urgent: moderate pain, fever with risk factors, worsening chronic conditions.
- Routine: stable chronic issues, follow-up visits without new alarming symptoms.
I will still ask the head nurse to validate the exact cut-offs and escalation rules before we say the protocol is final for D4.

The triage categories and examples in A3 look reasonable and align with typical outpatient practice.
For quality monitoring, it would help if the protocol also specifies:
- Expected maximum waiting time for each category.
- Documentation requirements in the EHR for T6 (for example, triage category field, escalation notes).
Once the head nurse confirms the thresholds, I am comfortable supporting approval of the triage protocol for D4.

For us at the desk, it would be useful if the triage protocol in A3 also indicates when we should alert nursing immediately at arrival, even before the usual queue, for example if a patient looks very unwell.
Maybe a short list of red-flag symptoms we can recognize without measuring vitals.

Good point. I will add a small section in A3 for front-desk red flags, such as visible breathing difficulty, confusion, or chest pain, with a simple instruction to call nursing immediately.
I will include this in the version I send to the head nurse for validation.

To close this loop:
- For the intake and consent forms in A2 (T2), we agree on the structure and mandatory fields as described, with grouped EHR-required fields, clear consent sections, and a privacy notice checkbox, pending final wording review by the compliance officer. This covers D3.
- For the triage protocol in A3 (T3), we agree on the three categories, example criteria, waiting time expectations, documentation requirements, and front-desk red flags, pending validation by the head nurse. This covers D4.
Next, 196511 will finalize the EHR alignment for T6 so we can avoid duplicate data entry.

threads.thread_goal: Define quality control approach and how audits and incidents will be handled.

messages.text:
I have prepared first drafts for the daily quality control checklist in A4 (T4) and the incident and improvement log template in A6 (T12).
Let us use this thread to agree on the daily audit routine, responsibilities, and minimum compliance threshold for D5, and on how incidents and suggestions will be logged and reviewed for D6.

Quick overview of A4 for T4:
- Section 1: front-desk checks (ID verified, mandatory fields completed on A2, consent recorded, EHR entries done for T6).
- Section 2: nursing checks (triage category recorded, vitals documented, escalation documented when applicable, use of A3).
- Section 3: timing checks (arrival time, triage time, any delays noted).
Each item is marked pass or fail, with space for comments.
For A6 and T12, the log has fields for date, shift, type of issue (data, timing, communication, safety), short description, immediate action, and follow-up owner.

From the admin side, A4 looks workable as long as the checklist is quick to complete.
For the daily audit routine in T9, I suggest:
- One short audit per shift, focusing on a small sample of patients.
- Rotating responsibility among front-desk and nursing staff, with support from you when needed.
We should also define what minimum compliance threshold we aim for so we know when to trigger extra training.

Agree that one audit per shift is realistic.
For the front-desk part of A4, could we pre-fill some items from the EHR for T6, for example by running a simple report, so the person doing the audit only has to spot-check a few records instead of checking everything manually?

For nursing, I think we can handle a short daily audit if it is limited to a few cases.
I would prefer if the checklist in A4 focuses on the most critical items: correct triage category, vitals recorded, and escalation documented when needed.
If we try to check too many details every day, it might be hard to keep up during busy shifts.

On the incident and improvement log in A6 for T12, I like that you separated issue type and follow-up owner.
For the review routine for D6, I suggest we:
- Have a short review twice a week to look at new entries and agree on quick fixes.
- Use the log to identify topics that need to be added to training materials or refreshers.
We should also make it easy for staff to record suggestions, not only problems.

From the desk perspective, I support one short audit per shift as long as the checklist in A4 is clear.
For incidents in A6, it would help if we can log them quickly, maybe with a simple dropdown for the most common issues, so people do not feel it is extra paperwork.

Based on your feedback, I propose the following for D5:
- Daily audits in T9: one per shift, sampling 3 to 5 patients.
- Responsibilities: each shift has a named person (front-desk or nurse) responsible for completing A4, with me available for questions.
- Minimum compliance threshold: we aim for at least 95 percent pass rate on critical items (ID, consent, triage category, vitals, escalation documentation). If we fall below that for more than two days in a row, we trigger a focused review and possibly extra training.
Does this sound acceptable, or is 95 percent too strict for the first weeks?

I like the structure. Maybe for the first two weeks we can accept a slightly lower threshold, say 90 percent, and then move to 95 percent once people are more familiar with the new process.
That way we still have a clear target but give some room for learning.

From the nursing side, starting at 90 percent and then aiming for 95 percent sounds more realistic, especially during the pilot.
The sample size of 3 to 5 patients per shift is fine.

On your idea about using EHR reports for T6, I can check with IT if we can get a simple daily list of patients with missing mandatory fields.
If that is possible, we could use it to pre-select cases for the audit in A4, which would save time.

For D6, building on your suggestion, I propose the following routine for A6 and T12:
- Staff record incidents and improvement ideas in A6 as they occur, using simple categories and short descriptions.
- Twice a week, we have a 15-minute async review in this channel where I summarize new entries and propose quick actions.
- More complex issues are flagged for discussion with operations or clinical leads.
This should keep the log active without overloading people.

That routine for A6 works for me and fits well with the idea of continuous learning.
We can also use patterns from the log to update training materials in T5 and the SOP in A7 later on.

I am comfortable with starting at 90 percent and then moving to 95 percent.
The key for us will be that the checklist in A4 is easy to understand and that we get quick feedback from the log in A6 so we see that our input leads to improvements.

Thanks all. To summarize for D5 and D6:
- Daily audits (T9) using A4: one per shift, 3 to 5 patients, focusing on critical items. Compliance threshold: 90 percent for the first two weeks after go-live, then 95 percent.
- Responsibilities: each shift has a named auditor; I will coordinate and support.
- Incident and improvement log (T12) in A6: staff record entries as they occur; we review twice a week in this channel and assign follow-up owners.
I will update A4 and A6 accordingly and share the revised versions.

threads.thread_goal: Plan training, communication, and pilot rollout details.

messages.text:
I have drafted the outline for the staff training materials in A5 (T5), a first version of the SOP structure in A7 (T10), and a proposal for patient-facing communication text in A8 (T11).
Let us use this thread to confirm the training schedule and format for D7, and to agree on the pilot start date, scope, and patient communication channels for D8.

Quick overview:
- A5 (T5): two slide decks, one for front-desk, one for nursing, plus one-page quick guides. Each covers the new workflow from A1, how to use A2 and A3, and how audits and logs in A4 and A6 will work.
- A7 (T10): SOP structure with sections on scope, roles, step-by-step workflow, links to forms and EHR instructions, and QC routines.
- A8 (T11): short text for posters and digital screens explaining the new check-in steps, expected information, and that we are standardizing to reduce waiting times.
I would like your input on how to schedule sessions across shifts for T7 and what format works best.

For T7, I suggest we plan short sessions of 30 minutes:
- Two sessions for front-desk staff (morning and afternoon) so everyone can attend around their shifts.
- Two sessions for nursing staff, possibly aligned with existing team meetings.
We can record one session per group and share the recording plus A5 as mandatory material for anyone who cannot attend live.
We should also define which parts are mandatory for each role for D7.

From the front-desk side, 30 minutes sounds reasonable.
For mandatory content for D7, I would say:
- For front-desk: new workflow overview from A1, how to use A2, basic understanding of A3 red flags, and how to handle audits and logs in A4 and A6.
- For nursing: they probably need more detail on A3 and less on the EHR admin side.
We should also include a short scenario exercise in A5 so people can practice a typical check-in.

For nursing, we can probably integrate one of the 30-minute sessions into our regular team meeting.
Mandatory content for us should be:
- Detailed triage protocol from A3.
- How to document in the EHR for T6.
- How the daily audits in A4 and the incident log in A6 will work.
I think a short case discussion in A5 would help make the triage rules more concrete.

I like the idea of recording one session. For those of us who might miss the live slot, could we also have a short quiz or checklist to confirm we went through the material in A5?
That might help ensure everyone is on the same page before the pilot.

Good idea. I can add a short self-check at the end of A5, with a few questions staff can use to verify they understood the key steps.
We can ask managers to confirm that their teams completed either the live session or the recording plus self-check.

From a quality standpoint, I would like the training to explicitly cover:
- Why we are introducing A4 and A6 and how they will be used, so people do not see them as extra bureaucracy.
- The minimum compliance thresholds we agreed in D5.
If we make this clear in A5 and A7, it should help with adoption.

On the pilot for T8 and D8, we need to pick a start date that aligns with the EHR maintenance window and gives us time to train everyone.
If we assume we can complete training in the next week, could we aim for a pilot start on the following Monday, limited to morning outpatient slots only for the first three days?
That would let us monitor closely and adjust before expanding.

Limiting the pilot to morning outpatient slots for the first three days sounds manageable from the nursing side.
We can make sure one of us is available as a point person during those mornings to support colleagues with the new triage protocol in A3 and the audits in A4.

From the front-desk side, starting with mornings only is a good idea.
For patient communication channels for D8, I suggest we use:
- Posters and small flyers based on A8 at the entrance and waiting area.
- A short message on the appointment reminders, if possible, mentioning that we are standardizing check-in to improve waiting times.
We should keep the message positive and simple.

Agree on posters and flyers.
Could we also have a very short script in A5 or A7 that front-desk staff can use to explain the new process to patients in a consistent way, especially on the first pilot days?

Yes, I can add a short script to A5 and reference it in A7, something like: 'We are using a new standardized check-in form today to make your visit smoother. It may take a few extra minutes the first time, but it will help us reduce waiting times in the future.'
I will also ensure the text in A8 matches this tone.

For the pilot in T8 and D8, I will prepare a simple checklist in A7 to confirm readiness two days before start: training completed, forms printed, A4 and A6 available, and EHR notes for T6 updated.
During the pilot mornings, I will monitor A6 closely and share a short summary at the end of each day.

To summarize for D7 and D8:
- Training (T5, T7): 30-minute sessions for front-desk and nursing, with separate decks in A5. Attendance is mandatory for all staff in scope; those who cannot attend must watch the recording and complete the self-check. Front-desk must cover A1, A2, front-desk parts of A3, A4, and A6; nursing must cover A3, EHR documentation for T6, A4, and A6.
- Pilot (T8): start on the agreed Monday, mornings only for the first three days, using the new workflow, forms, triage protocol, and QC tools. Patient communication via posters and flyers from A8 and a short script in A5/A7.
If there are no objections, we will proceed with this plan.
No objections from me. The plan for training and the pilot scope is clear and workable from the nursing side.

All good from the front-desk perspective as well.
I will coordinate with 438229 to make sure everyone is booked into one of the sessions and knows where to find A5 and A8.
